readings.title: Winnie-the-Pooh: the Introduction
readings.challenge: Listen for the author talking straight to you, and for his jokes.
readings.focus: Milne explains a name, admits what he has forgotten, and lets Piglet interrupt him.
readings.context: A. A. Milne wrote this introduction to Winnie-the-Pooh (1926), a book about his son Christopher Robin and his toy animals. The “other book about Christopher Robin” is Milne’s book of poems, When We Were Very Young. Winnie was a real bear at the London Zoo. “A. A. M.” are Milne’s initials.

excerpt.locator: The author’s Introduction, the whole of it; opens “If you happen to have read another book about Christopher Robin, you may remember that he…”; closes “A. A. M.”.

questions.prompt: Where did the “Pooh” part of the name come from?
facilitatorNotes: From a swan Christopher Robin used to call Pooh; when they said good-bye to the swan they kept the name. Milne even jokes that perhaps the swan had Christopher Robin.
evidence: he used to call this swan Pooh

questions.prompt: How does Christopher Robin visit the Zoo differently from people who walk from WAYIN to WAYOUT?
facilitatorNotes: He goes straight to the animal he loves most and stays there; Milne calls those “the nicest people.” Ask how the child would visit.
evidence: the nicest people go straight to the animal they love the most, and stay there

questions.prompt: Why is Piglet jealous, and what is good about being small, according to Milne?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks Pooh is getting a Grand Introduction all to himself. Being small, Piglet fits in a pocket and gets taken to school.
evidence: Piglet is so small that he slips into a pocket

questions.prompt: Is twice seven twelve or twenty-two? Why does Milne put a wrong sum in?
facilitatorNotes: Neither: it is fourteen. The joke shows a child unsure of a sum at school, which is just when a Piglet in your pocket is comforting.
evidence: whether twice seven is twelve or twenty-two

readings.title: The Expotition to the North Pole — Pooh’s song and the Big Boots
readings.challenge: Notice when Pooh pretends to understand a word he doesn’t know.
readings.focus: A song that has to stay true, and a big word nobody is quite sure of.
readings.context: From Chapter VIII of A. A. Milne’s Winnie-the-Pooh (1926). Christopher Robin is a boy, and Pooh and his friends are his toy animals, alive in the stories. An expedition is a journey to explore or find something; Pooh calls it an “Expotition.” Provisions are food packed for a journey. The North Pole is a real place, the farthest point north on Earth, across frozen sea.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from the start to Pooh setting off to tell the others; opens “One fine day Pooh had stumped up to the top of the Forest to see if his friend…”; closes “…Pooh happily. "I thought you said Provisions. I'll go and tell them." And he stumped off.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Pooh turn his song into a hum?
facilitatorNotes: If he keeps singing it will be time for “a little something,” and then the last line won’t be true. He wants his song to stay true.
evidence: it will be time for the little something, and then the last line won't be true

questions.prompt: What does Pooh know as soon as he sees the Big Boots?
facilitatorNotes: That an Adventure is coming. He brushes the honey off his nose to look Ready for Anything.
evidence: As soon as he saw the Big Boots, Pooh knew that an Adventure was going to happen

questions.prompt: Pooh says “I know,” but he doesn’t really. Who else isn’t quite sure what a word means?
facilitatorNotes: Christopher Robin: he calls the North Pole “just a thing you discover” because he is not quite sure himself.
evidence: said Christopher Robin carelessly, not being quite sure himself

questions.prompt: Pooh says, “I thought you said Provisions.” Why is that funny?
facilitatorNotes: Christopher Robin did say Provisions. Pooh acts as if the explanation were what he had known all along.
evidence: I thought you said Provisions.

readings.title: The Expotition to the North Pole — passing the message along
readings.challenge: Follow a message as it changes from one animal to the next.
readings.focus: Each friend takes the news differently: Rabbit plays with it, Piglet worries, and Eeyore grumbles.
readings.context: Recap: Christopher Robin is leading an “Expotition” to discover the North Pole, though he is not sure what it is, and Pooh has gone to tell everyone to bring Provisions, which means things to eat. Rabbit’s friends-and-relations are his many small animal relatives. “Here we go gathering Nuts and May” is an old ring game.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from Pooh meeting Rabbit to Pooh’s song about the Pole; opens “The first person he met was Rabbit.”; closes “…too— And where the Pole was none of them knew.... Sing Hey! for Owl and Rabbit and all!”.

questions.prompt: What does Pooh tell Rabbit an Expotition is, and what does he say they will discover?
facilitatorNotes: “A sort of boat,” and a Pole, or perhaps a Mole. The message is already changing as it travels.
evidence: A sort of boat, I think
Or was it a Mole?

questions.prompt: What worries Piglet, and what makes him feel better?
facilitatorNotes: Something fierce with teeth; but if Christopher Robin is coming he doesn’t mind anything.
evidence: It isn't their necks I mind
But if Christopher Robin is coming I don't mind anything.

questions.prompt: Why does Eeyore say this isn’t an Expo-whatever at all, but “simply a Confused Noise”?
facilitatorNotes: Rabbit’s relations crowd the end of the line, so he has to brush them away to sit down. Some children will agree it is a muddle; others will say Eeyore always finds something to grumble about.
evidence: it's simply a Confused Noise

questions.prompt: Pooh’s song says nobody knew where the Pole was. Is the song right?
facilitatorNotes: Yes, and that is the joke: the song is truer than anyone will admit out loud. Enjoy the rhyme of “Pole” and “tole.”
evidence: where the Pole was none of them knew

readings.title: The Expotition to the North Pole — Hush, an Ambush, and a quiet question
readings.challenge: Listen to “Hush!” travel down the line, and notice what happens at the very end.
readings.focus: Big words cause small muddles, and even the leaders keep a secret: they don’t know what they are looking for.
readings.context: Recap: the whole Expotition, from Christopher Robin at the front to Rabbit’s smallest relations at the back, has set off to discover the North Pole, and Pooh has made up a song about it. An ambush is a surprise attack from a hiding place. Gorse is a prickly bush, and a thistle is a prickly plant that donkeys like to eat.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from the “Hush!” passed down the line to Christopher Robin’s talk with Rabbit; opens “"Hush!" said Christopher Robin turning round to Pooh, "we're just coming to a Dangerous…”; closes “"That's what we're looking for," said Christopher Robin.”.

questions.prompt: What happens to the very last and smallest friend-and-relation when everyone says “Hush!” to him?
facilitatorNotes: He buries himself head down for two days and then goes home to live quietly with his Aunt. A small word grows frightening by the end of the line.
evidence: His name was Alexander Beetle.

questions.prompt: Pooh thinks an Ambush might be a gorse-bush. Is he completely wrong?
facilitatorNotes: A gorse-bush once “sprang” at him when he fell, so in Pooh’s way he has a point, which annoys Owl. Some children will side with Pooh, some with Owl.
evidence: So is a gorse-bush sometimes

questions.prompt: Eeyore gets Pooh’s thistle and then talks about “Thought for Others.” Why is that funny?
facilitatorNotes: He is the one who just took Pooh’s seat and lunch, yet he lectures everyone else on thinking of others.
evidence: A little Consideration, a little Thought for Others, makes all the difference.

questions.prompt: Why does Christopher Robin take Rabbit aside? What do they both pretend?
facilitatorNotes: He doesn’t want the others to hear that he doesn’t know what the North Pole looks like. Both pretend they knew once and forgot.
evidence: I didn't want the others to hear
I did know once, only I've sort of forgotten

readings.title: The Expotition to the North Pole — Roo falls in and Pooh finds the Pole
readings.challenge: Notice what each friend does when Roo falls in, and who actually helps.
readings.focus: An ordinary pole, picked up to rescue a friend, becomes a great discovery.
readings.context: Recap: the Expotition has stopped beside a stream to eat its Provisions. Christopher Robin and Rabbit have agreed that the North Pole is probably “just a pole stuck in the ground,” but nobody knows where. Immersion means falling into water. To revive is to bring back strength.
readings.contentNote: Little Roo falls into the stream and is swept over two small waterfalls before he is pulled out safe.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from the return to the others to the end of the chapter; opens “They went back to the others. Piglet was lying on his back, sleeping peacefully. Roo was…”; closes “…and feeling very proud of what he had done, had a little something to revive himself.”.

questions.prompt: What does each friend do when Roo falls in? Whose help works?
facilitatorNotes: Piglet jumps and squeaks, Owl gives advice, Kanga runs along the bank, Eeyore hangs his tail in the water, Christopher Robin and Rabbit rush about. Pooh and Kanga hold a pole across the stream, and Roo climbs out.
evidence: Two pools below Roo he was standing with a long pole in his paws

questions.prompt: What does Roo keep saying in the water? How does he feel about falling in?
facilitatorNotes: “Look at me swimming!” He is proud, not frightened, while Kanga is anxious.
evidence: Look at me swimming!

questions.prompt: Why does Christopher Robin say Pooh has found the North Pole?
facilitatorNotes: They decided the Pole would be a pole stuck in the ground, and Pooh has found a pole. Some children will think Christopher Robin believes it; others that he knows better and wants to honour Pooh. Both fit.
evidence: You have found the North Pole!

questions.prompt: Eeyore says, “Well, anyhow—it didn’t rain.” What does that show about how he sees things?
facilitatorNotes: He is not impressed, or he always expects the worst and is surprised by a small good thing. Ask which sounds more like the Eeyore they know.
evidence: Well, anyhow—it didn't rain

readings.title: Piglet Entirely Surrounded by Water — the message in a bottle
readings.challenge: Listen to Piglet think about each friend and what that friend would do.
readings.focus: A very small animal alone in a flood worries, thinks, and does the one thing he can.
readings.context: From Chapter IX of A. A. Milne’s Winnie-the-Pooh (1926). Christopher Robin is a boy, and Pooh, Piglet and their friends are his toy animals, alive in the stories. Piglet is very small. A flood is when rain makes rivers spill over onto the land. Anxious means worried. A desert island is a lonely island in the sea, and a cork is a stopper for a bottle. Milne gives Important Words capital letters to show how big they feel to Piglet.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, from the start to Piglet wishing Pooh were there; opens “It rained and it rained and it rained. Piglet told himself that never in all his life,…”; closes “…a very long sigh and said, "I wish Pooh were here. It's so much more friendly with two."”.

questions.prompt: How does each friend escape a flood, in Piglet’s mind? Why can’t Piglet do any of those?
facilitatorNotes: Climbing trees, jumping, burrowing, flying, or making a loud noise until rescued. Piglet is too small and can do none of them.
evidence: here am I, surrounded by water and I can't do anything

questions.prompt: What does Piglet say about Pooh, Owl, Rabbit and Kanga? Do you agree with him?
facilitatorNotes: Pooh does silly things that turn out right; Owl Knows Things; Rabbit thinks of Clever Plans; Kanga does the Good Thing without thinking. Let children add what they know of each friend.
evidence: He does silly things and they turn out right.

questions.prompt: What does Piglet write on the paper? Why does he write “(ME)”?
facilitatorNotes: “HELP! PIGLET (ME)” and “IT’S ME PIGLET, HELP HELP.” He wants to be quite sure whoever finds it knows it is him.
evidence: PIGLET (ME)

questions.prompt: Piglet says, “It’s so much more friendly with two.” Why might being alone feel worse than the water?
facilitatorNotes: The flood is even rather exciting, but nothing is fun without someone to share it with. Some children will say the water is still the scariest part; both are in the text.
evidence: it wasn't much good having anything exciting like floods, if you couldn't share them with somebody
It's so much more friendly with two.

readings.title: Piglet Entirely Surrounded by Water — Pooh’s Escape and The Floating Bear
readings.challenge: Count Pooh’s honey pots as the days go by.
readings.focus: Pooh saves his honey first, then finds a bottle, a message and a very wobbly boat.
readings.context: Recap: it has rained for days, and Piglet, alone in his house with water up to his window, wrote “HELP! PIGLET (ME)” on a paper, put it in a bottle, and threw it into the flood. In the chapter before this one, Pooh found what Christopher Robin called the North Pole, and here he sets out to find an East Pole. Woozles are imaginary creatures Pooh worries about. Astride means sitting with a leg on each side.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, from Pooh asleep when the rain began to Pooh paddling The Floating Bear; opens “When the rain began Pooh was asleep. It rained, and it rained, and it rained, and he…”; closes “…Bear underneath and Pooh triumphantly astride it, paddling vigorously with his feet.”.

questions.prompt: What wakes Pooh up? What is he dreaming about?
facilitatorNotes: Cold water around his feet. He dreams that Woozles at the East Pole are nibbling the fur off his legs to make nests, so his legs get colder and colder.
evidence: he woke up with an Ow!—and there he was, sitting in his chair with his feet in the water

questions.prompt: What does Pooh take with him for his Escape? What happens to it day by day?
facilitatorNotes: His honey: ten pots at first, then four, then one, then none, because he eats it.
evidence: were ten pots of honey....
was one pot of honey.

questions.prompt: Pooh can’t read the message. Why does he think it is for him?
facilitatorNotes: The letter “P” is in it, and he thinks P means Pooh, but it stands for Piglet.
evidence: and 'P' means 'Pooh,' so it's a very important Missage to me

questions.prompt: The storyteller says Pooh’s boat was a good idea “for a Bear of Very Little Brain.” Is that praise, or teasing, or both?
facilitatorNotes: Both: it really is clever to think a jar can float like a bottle, and the boat still keeps turning over. Children may decide either way, with words to show it.
evidence: If a bottle can float, then a jar can float,
uncertain as to which of them was meant to be on the top

readings.title: Piglet Entirely Surrounded by Water — Owl’s long words and Pooh’s Missage
readings.challenge: Listen for each long word Owl uses, and what it means in short words.
readings.focus: Christopher Robin worries about Pooh, Pooh arrives, and the message at last is read.
readings.context: Recap: in the flood, Piglet sent a message in a bottle saying “HELP! PIGLET (ME).” Pooh found the bottle, could not read the message, and paddled off on a honey jar he named The Floating Bear to find a Clever Reader. Christopher Robin lives at the top of the Forest, and Owl likes to use long words.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, from Christopher Robin on his island to Owl flying off to Piglet; opens “Christopher Robin lived at the very top of the Forest. It rained, and it rained, and it…”; closes “…Oh, don't talk, Owl, go on quick!" And, still thinking of something to say, Owl flew off.”.

questions.prompt: How does Christopher Robin know he is on a real island?
facilitatorNotes: Every morning he marks the water with a stick, and each day the water is higher; on the fifth morning there is water all round him.
evidence: knew that for the first time in his life he was on a real island

questions.prompt: What does Owl mean by “atmospheric conditions” and “unprecedented height”? Why does he say it the long way?
facilitatorNotes: It has been raining, and there is a lot of water. He likes to sound wise, and he keeps trying to finish his long sentence.
evidence: It has been raining,
There's a lot of water about,

questions.prompt: What does Christopher Robin say about Pooh that tells you how he feels?
facilitatorNotes: That Pooh might do something silly, and “I do love him so.”
evidence: and I do love him so, Owl

questions.prompt: When Pooh hears the message is from Piglet, he asks, “Isn’t there anything about Pooh in it?” What does that show?
facilitatorNotes: He is a little disappointed it is not for him, and still thinking of himself; then he understands the P’s. Some children will say he is just funny, not selfish. Both fit.
evidence: Isn't there anything about Pooh in it?
Oh, are those 'P's' piglets? I thought they were poohs.

readings.title: Piglet Entirely Surrounded by Water — The Brain of Pooh
readings.challenge: Listen for how Christopher Robin answers without any words at all.
readings.focus: Pooh has a truly clever idea, and the rescue boat is named after his brain.
readings.context: Recap: Piglet, alone and surrounded by flood water, sent a message in a bottle. Pooh found it and paddled his honey jar, The Floating Bear, to Christopher Robin, who read “HELP! PIGLET (ME)” and sent Owl ahead to say Rescue is Coming. Modestly means without showing off. A ship’s Mate helps the Captain. Revolving means turning round and round.
readings.contentNote: Piglet nearly slips out of his window into the water while he dozes, and wakes just in time.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, from Christopher Robin asking where Pooh’s boat is to the end of the chapter; opens “"Now then, Pooh," said Christopher Robin, "where's your boat?"”; closes “…of the story, and I am very tired after that last sentence, I think I shall stop there.”.

questions.prompt: Why can’t they use Pooh’s boat?
facilitatorNotes: It is too small for two, and smaller still for three with Piglet; and it is sometimes more of an Accident than a Boat.
evidence: Sometimes it's a Boat, and sometimes it's more of an Accident.

questions.prompt: What is Pooh’s idea? How does Christopher Robin answer at first?
facilitatorNotes: To go in Christopher Robin’s umbrella. He answers with question marks, then exclamation marks, as he slowly sees it will work. Read them as faces or noises.
evidence: We might go in your umbrella,

questions.prompt: Why does Christopher Robin name the boat “The Brain of Pooh”?
facilitatorNotes: To honour Pooh’s clever idea, the Bear of Very Little Brain who thought of it.
evidence: I shall call this boat The Brain of Pooh

questions.prompt: Owl’s long story almost puts Piglet in danger. What is funny about it?
facilitatorNotes: Owl came to comfort him, but his story is so long that Piglet falls asleep and nearly slips into the water; the storyteller even makes his own sentence long like Owl’s story. Some children will notice Piglet later likes to tell it as a Very Great Danger.
evidence: the story went on and on, rather like this sentence
